title: Evaluating Biotechnology: Mosquito-borne Disease
subtitle: Gene drives, Wolbachia and a five-move framework for evaluating any biotechnology
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: (ACSBL087)
analysing the social implications and ethical uses of biotechnology, including plant and animal examples
Conduct a secondary-source investigation to evaluate the use of biotechnologies on the prevalence of mosquito-borne diseases
Evaluate the potential societal benefits of using genetic technologies to manage infectious diseases
Evaluate the release of a genetically modified organism into the wild and predict the impacts on natural populations
inquiryQuestion: How do genetic techniques affect Earth's biodiversity?
lessonIntent: Students can evaluate biotechnologies used against mosquito-borne disease (gene drives, Wolbachia, sterile or self-limiting males) using trial data and a five-move framework ending in a conditional conclusion.
examSkill: Structure an extended-response evaluation of a biotechnology using data on disease prevalence and five moves, rather than listing facts or picking a one-sided verdict.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, evaluating biotechnologies against mosquito borne disease. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Would you release a gene drive?
scenes.body: Mosquitoes spread malaria and dengue to hundreds of millions of people a year. Gene-drive mosquitoes could crash the populations that carry malaria, but a gene drive spreads through the wild and cannot be recalled.
scenes.callout: A powerful benefit and an irreversible risk in the same decision.
scenes.caption: Mosquito-borne disease is a real test case for evaluating biotechnology, not a slogan.

voiceover.text: Malaria alone causes around a quarter of a billion cases every year, and dengue, spread by a different mosquito, is surging across the tropics. So scientists have turned to biotechnology. The Target Malaria project is developing gene drive mosquitoes designed to crash the populations of the species that spread malaria. In twenty nineteen, in Burkina Faso, it made the first release of genetically modified mosquitoes in Africa, a sterile male strain with no gene drive, as a careful first step. Here's what makes a gene drive so hard to judge. A normal gene is inherited by about half the offspring, but a gene drive forces itself into nearly all of them, so it sweeps through a wild population and cannot be recalled. Enormous benefit, irreversible risk, in one decision. You can't answer that with a slogan, so today you'll get the five move framework the markers are really after.

scenes.heading: Three biotechnologies against mosquito-borne disease
scenes.body: Each approach aims to lower disease prevalence by changing the mosquito population, but they work very differently.

bullets.text: Gene drive: a CRISPR-based gene spreads to nearly all offspring and can crash the population.
Wolbachia: a natural bacterium stops Aedes mosquitoes passing on dengue.
Sterile or self-limiting males: released males mate, but their eggs fail to hatch or their daughters die.

scenes.secondary: Only the gene drive keeps spreading by itself. Wolbachia spreads through the population too, but it is a natural bacterium, not a genetic modification. Sterile male releases fade away unless they are repeated.
scenes.callout: Ask of each one: how does it lower transmission, and can it be recalled?
scenes.caption: Gene drives, Wolbachia and sterile males lower mosquito-borne disease in different ways.
scenes.recapSeed: Gene drive, Wolbachia and sterile males each cut transmission differently.

voiceover.text: Before we evaluate, let's line up the main biotechnologies, because they work very differently. First, gene drives, which we've met. A CRISPR based drive spreads a gene, often one that disrupts female fertility, into nearly all offspring, so the population can collapse. In caged trials this has worked, but so far gene drives have been tested mainly in the lab, not in the wild. Second, Wolbachia, a natural bacterium that, when it's put into the Aedes mosquitoes that carry dengue, stops them passing the virus on. It's an Australian led approach, from the World Mosquito Program, and it spreads through the wild population by itself. And third, sterile or self limiting males. Huge numbers of males are released, they mate with wild females, and either the eggs never hatch or, in the self limiting kind, the female offspring die before adulthood, so the population drops. That effect fades unless you keep releasing. So for each one, ask how it lowers transmission, and whether it can be recalled.

scenes.heading: Reading the data: Wolbachia in Yogyakarta
scenes.body: A randomised trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, compared dengue in city areas with and without Wolbachia mosquitoes.

bullets.text: Untreated areas: about 8.5% of participants had confirmed dengue.
Wolbachia areas: about 2.3% had confirmed dengue.
That is a 77% reduction, and 86% fewer dengue hospitalisations.

scenes.secondary: This was a cluster randomised controlled trial, the strongest design for showing that the biotechnology, not something else, lowered the prevalence of disease.
scenes.callout: A randomised design lets you link the drop in dengue to the Wolbachia itself.
scenes.caption: In Yogyakarta, Wolbachia areas had 77% less dengue than untreated areas.

voiceover.text: Now let's use real data, because an evaluation needs evidence, not just ideas. In Yogyakarta, in Indonesia, researchers divided the city into areas and randomly chose which ones received Wolbachia mosquitoes. Then they tracked people with fevers and tested them for dengue. In the untreated areas, about eight point five percent of participants had confirmed dengue. In the Wolbachia areas, it was about two point three percent. That works out to a seventy seven percent reduction, and dengue hospitalisations fell by eighty six percent. And here's why the design matters. Because the areas were randomly assigned, other differences between neighbourhoods should balance out, so the fall in dengue can be linked to the Wolbachia itself. That's the kind of evidence that lets you say a biotechnology actually changed the prevalence of a disease.

scenes.heading: The five-move evaluation
scenes.body: A complete evaluation is not a list of facts. It runs five moves in order and ends with a position.

bullets.text: Move 1: identify the benefit clearly and specifically.
Move 2: describe the risk or limitation.
Move 3: analyse stakeholder impact, who gains and who bears the cost.
Move 4: assess the biodiversity effect at a named level.
Move 5: reach a conditional conclusion, not a slogan.

scenes.secondary: The strongest answers are conditional, not one-sided. A catalogue of facts without a judgement stays in the middle bands.
scenes.callout: Five moves, in order, always ending on a stated position.
scenes.caption: Five moves: benefit, risk, stakeholder impact, biodiversity level, conditional conclusion.

voiceover.text: Here's the framework, and it works for any biotechnology they throw at you. A complete evaluation runs five moves in order. Move one, identify the benefit clearly and specifically, not just it helps people. Move two, describe the risk or limitation honestly. Move three, analyse stakeholder impact, because the same technology affects different groups differently, ask who gains and who carries the cost. Move four, assess the biodiversity effect at a named level, genetic, species or ecosystem, exactly as we practised with biodiversity. And move five, reach a conditional conclusion, a stated position, not a slogan. The key insight is that the strongest answers are conditional rather than one sided, and a pile of facts with no judgement stays stuck in the middle bands.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Synthesis: combining several ideas and examples into one coherent judgement.
Evidence-based evaluation: a judgement backed by examples and conditions, not absolutes.
Trade-off: a benefit that comes linked to a cost, risk or competing consequence.
Stakeholder impact: how different groups are affected differently by the same technology.
Qualified judgement: a conclusion using conditional language such as in some contexts or provided that.

scenes.callout: Synthesis and qualified judgement earn the top marks, not recall.
scenes.caption: Synthesis, evidence-based evaluation, trade-off, stakeholder impact, qualified judgement.

voiceover.text: Five terms underpin this. Synthesis is combining several ideas and examples into one coherent judgement, rather than treating them as separate dot points. Evidence based evaluation is a judgement supported by relevant examples, conditions and limitations, not by sweeping absolutes. A trade off is a situation where a benefit comes linked to a cost, a risk or a competing consequence, and almost every biotechnology has one. Stakeholder impact is the idea that the same technology affects different groups differently, a farmer, a patient and a seed company do not all experience it the same way. And a qualified judgement is a conclusion that uses conditional language, phrases like in some contexts, or provided that. Synthesis and qualified judgement are what actually earn the top marks, not recall.

scenes.heading: Different domains, different issues
scenes.body: You cannot force one universal verdict. Medical, agricultural and animal biotech raise different concerns.

bullets.text: Medical: access, cost, safety and consent.
Agricultural: ownership, monoculture and biodiversity trade-offs.

scenes.secondary: Compare cases on their own terms. A response that judges insulin and gene drives by the same single rule will miss the specific issues each one raises.
scenes.callout: Match the issues to the domain before you conclude.
scenes.caption: Medical, agricultural and animal biotechnology each raise distinct evaluation issues.

voiceover.text: Now a refinement that lifts an answer. You cannot force one universal verdict across every kind of biotechnology, because different domains raise different issues. Medical biotechnology tends to raise questions of access, cost, safety and consent, who can afford it and did they agree to it. Agricultural biotechnology raises ownership, monoculture and biodiversity trade offs, including who owns the seed. And animal biotechnology raises welfare, necessity and harm, is the suffering justified. So compare cases on their own terms. An answer that judges insulin production and a gene drive by the exact same single rule will simply miss the specific issues each one actually raises.

scenes.heading: Apply the framework to gene drives
scenes.question: Use the five-move framework to evaluate releasing gene-drive mosquitoes to suppress malaria. Work through benefit, risk, stakeholders, biodiversity level, then a conditional conclusion.
scenes.coachNote: Hit all five moves. The mark is lost by skipping stakeholders or ending without a position.
steps: Benefit: suppressing the vector population could sharply cut malaria, which causes around a quarter of a billion cases a year.
Risk: a gene drive spreads through nearly all offspring instead of half, so the change is self-propagating and cannot be recalled.
Stakeholders: communities gain disease relief, but neighbouring regions and ecosystems inherit an irreversible change they did not choose.
Biodiversity level: removing one mosquito species could affect the animals that feed on it, an ecosystem-level effect that is hard to predict.
Conclusion: justified only under strict regulation, staged trials and community consent, because the benefit is large but the risk is irreversible.
scenes.caption: A five-move evaluation of gene drives ends in a conditional, regulated conclusion.

voiceover.text: Let's run all five moves on the gene drive case. Move one, benefit, suppressing the mosquito population could sharply cut malaria, which causes around a quarter of a billion cases a year, so the upside is enormous. Move two, risk, the gene drive spreads through nearly all of the offspring instead of half, so it is self propagating and cannot be recalled once it's out. Move three, stakeholders, affected communities gain real relief from disease, but neighbouring regions and countries inherit an irreversible change they never agreed to. Move four, biodiversity, removing one mosquito species could affect the animals that feed on it, an ecosystem level effect that is hard to predict. And move five, the conditional conclusion, this is justified only under strict regulation, staged trials and genuine community consent, because the benefit is large but the risk is irreversible. Notice that every move is present, and it ends on a clear position.

scenes.heading: The big evaluation trap
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking a thorough answer just lists all the relevant facts. Listing is not evaluating.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: ending with there are pros and cons and stopping there, with no stated position. Trap 3: judging by production alone, biotechnology is good because it increases output, which confuses productivity with biodiversity.
scenes.mistakeTag: Why fact-dumps stall in the middle bands
scenes.callout: Analyse and judge; a list with no verdict caps your marks.
scenes.caption: Listing facts is not evaluating; finish with a stated, qualified position.

voiceover.text: Three traps that keep good students out of the top band. Trap one, the big one, thinking a thorough response just lists all the relevant facts. It does not, listing is not evaluating, and a catalogue of true statements with no analysis stays mid range. High scoring answers analyse evidence, identify trade offs and limitations, weigh different stakeholders, and then reach a supported judgement. Trap two, ending with there are pros and cons, and stopping, with no actual position. That sits on the fence and the markers see straight through it, you have to commit using qualified language. And trap three, judging by production alone, biotechnology is good because it increases output, which we already know confuses productivity with biodiversity. Analyse, then judge, that's the whole game here.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A student ends an evaluation of Wolbachia mosquitoes with: in conclusion, there are benefits and also some risks, so it is a complex issue. Why does this cap their marks, and how should they fix it?
answerSteps: The conclusion says there are pros and cons but never reaches a position, which is the fence-sitting trap.
Top bands need a qualified judgement using evidence and conditional language.
A fix uses the data and names the key condition, then commits.
For example: Wolbachia is justified in dengue areas, because a randomised trial showed 77% less dengue, provided long-term monitoring continues.
Answer: replace the non-committal ending with a conditional, evidence-based judgement.
scenes.caption: A fence-sitting conclusion must become a conditional, evidence-based judgement.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A student ends their evaluation of Wolbachia mosquitoes like this, in conclusion, there are benefits and also some risks, so it is a complex issue. Why does that cap their marks, and how should they fix it? Pause and reason it through. Okay, here's the issue. The conclusion lists that there are pros and cons, but it never actually reaches a position, that's the classic fence sitting trap. The top bands want a qualified judgement backed by evidence, not a restatement that the topic is complicated. The fix is to use the data, name the key condition, and then commit. Something like, Wolbachia is justified in areas with dengue, because a randomised trial showed seventy seven percent less dengue, provided that its long term effects keep being monitored. That commits to a position, uses evidence, and stays conditional.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Gene drives, Wolbachia and sterile males lower mosquito-borne disease in different ways.
Only a gene drive keeps spreading by itself and cannot be recalled.
Use data: Wolbachia cut dengue by 77% in a randomised trial.
Run five moves: benefit, risk, stakeholders, biodiversity level, conclusion.
End with a conditional, evidence-based position, never a fence-sit.
scenes.finalPrompt: Evaluating a biotechnology? Use the data, run five moves, then commit with conditional language.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: three approaches, reversibility, the data, five moves, a committed conclusion.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, gene drives, Wolbachia and sterile males all target mosquito borne disease, but they work in different ways. Second, only a gene drive keeps spreading through the wild by itself, which is why it can't be recalled. Third, use data when you evaluate, like the Yogyakarta trial where Wolbachia cut dengue by seventy seven percent. Fourth, run the five moves, benefit, risk, stakeholders, biodiversity level, and conclusion. And fifth, end every evaluation with a conditional, evidence based position, never a slogan and never a fence sit. Whenever you evaluate a biotechnology, use the data, run the five moves, then commit. See you next lesson.
